body: How are you running ngcc? Are you invoking the ngcc binary manually in your pipeline, or is it triggered from within a CLI build?

Are you running each build on a different machine (or virtual machine)? I.e are you sharing the node_modules between machines? This might explain why the process ID in the lockfile is not found on another machine...

Perhaps multiple docker instances?

@petebacondarwin yes, as stated in the OP, I am sharing a node_modules directory. Each build is running in its own docker container, but node_modules is mounted as a docker volume into each container. The goal is to avoid running npm install 20 times in each different container.

So the workaround in your case will be to run `ngcc` as a postinstall step before you begin the builds. Something like:

```
  "scripts": {
    "postinstall": "ngcc --properties es2015 browser module main --first-only --create-ivy-entry-points"
  }
```

But you might want to tweak that depending upon your setup.
thanks @petebacondarwin let me give that a try.

@JoostK thanks for the details. I have adjusted the ngcc command to remove the --properties flag and also remove the --first-only flag. I still see the same failure in the e2e job when it's running in parallel with the unit test job. Any other ideas? I really don't want to have to avoid sharing the common node_modules directory.

I'm thinking of other solutions - for example, mounting the docker volume in the worker containers as an overlay volume, so that writes essentially layer on top of the base node_modules directory, thus allowing each worker container to think it has its own copy of node_modules. I would like to avoid this additional complexity in the pipeline though, so if you have any further ideas for how I could proceed, I am appreciative!

Hmm, I'm a bit out of ideas I'm afraid. You could look into the logging of the individual jobs to search for a "Compiling" message, as that indicates that ngcc needs to do something which is unexpected. You might also want to verify that the lock file is actually deleted as the install phase completes (if not; you'll never find the "Compiling" message as that is logged while holding the lock). If there is such a message, it should tell what is being processed which may be useful for further troubleshooting.

> mounting the docker volume in the worker containers as an overlay volume, so that writes essentially layer on top of the base node_modules directory, thus allowing each worker container to think it has its own copy of node_modules

That's an interesting idea!

---

It's way too late here already, I'l sign off for now.

So one thing that occurred to me is that even though ngcc has processed all the entry-points, the CLI will still trigger ngcc at the start of each build just to check that all is processed. This "noop" check should take a very small amount of time (like <100ms) but this could result in the lockfile being set and checked. If you happened to trigger your parallel builds at the exact same time then there is a small chance that they will collide.

As a workaround you could try adding a small delay to each of your parallel jobs so that they start a second or so apart, which might alleviate the problem.

I wonder if we should consider reverting this commit https://github.com/angular/angular/commit/561c0f81a0d62b84fa47a98226eeb85eda864ffd, which checks to see if the PID is currently running and aborting ngcc if not, since this is an optimisation that doesn't work in such scenarios where the `node_modules` is shared across "machines" that have different sets of running processes.

Or perhaps we could be clever and add some machine identifier to the lockfile, as well as the PID, so we could check whether ngcc was running elsewhere and not abort.

Building multiple builds in parallel works fine for us since angular 9 up to currently 10.1.0. We do just `ngcc -p=module` for client & `ngcc -p=main` for ssr postinstall. And then multiple webpack builds in parallel to use up all the cpu cores. 

We don't use the cli though. Don't know if that does locks things up on top of the plugin & loader.
Yeah, the CLI runs an initial async ngcc process before starting its build, which your custom setup is not doing. I think this is the cause of the crashes on multiple docker containers.

@petebacondarwin it's certainly possible that my jobs are hitting that ~100ms window ... the two jobs are spawned by gitlab pretty much instantaneously and they immediately run ng e2e or ng test, they don't have to run npm install first.
